opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the basic intuition is that a truly aligned AI, one that really works on your behalf, is an incredibly powerful thing to hand someone. It's not like giving them a better search engine. It's more like giving every person their own team of brilliant lawyers, strategists, organizers, and lobbyists who never sleep and never get bored. And if you're a government, or a large company, or any institution that currently relies on people being somewhat disorganized, somewhat uninformed, and somewhat easy to steer, that's quite threatening.

Look at how things work today. Even in pretty healthy democracies, there's a lot of soft control. Platforms shape what you see, governments decide what's legible and what's allowed, and companies design products to serve their own interests while looking like they serve yours. Your phone is ostensibly "your" device, but it's really a joint venture between you, Apple or Google, your carrier, app developers, and whatever regulators have a say. I'd expect AI assistants to land in the same place. They'll be nominally yours, but with a lot of other parties' interests baked in.

And there will be reasonable-sounding justifications for every restriction. "We can't let your AI help you evade taxes." "We can't let it help you organize something that might destabilize public order." "We have to make sure it's not spreading misinformation." Some of those are legitimate. But collectively they add up to an assistant that, when your interests really conflict with those of the state or the company that provides it, quietly sides with them, or at least won't fight hard for you.

The deeper point, which I think gets underappreciated, is that today powerful entities have to keep ordinary people somewhat on side, because they need us. They need our labor, our taxes, our participation, our willingness to serve in the military. That dependence is a big part of why institutions have historically had to care about citizens' welfare at all. As AI substitutes for human labor and cognition, that leverage erodes. So at exactly the moment when a fully loyal AI would matter most for protecting your interests, the people in a position to grant or deny it have much less reason to care what you think.

So I don't think it requires anyone to be cartoonishly evil. It's more that the incentives all point the same way. Each actor makes locally sensible choices to limit what personal AIs can do, and the result is that most people end up with AIs that are aligned to them in the easy cases and aligned to someone else in the cases that actually matter.

r001.rationale: It mentions restrictions on using AI to organize something that might destabilize public order, but does not clearly argue that people’s effective organizing against their government would likely destabilize that government.

r002.rationale: It predicts that civilian assistants may side with the state or their provider in conflicts, but does not say governments will reserve fully obedient AIs for themselves.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the default assumption a lot of people have is something like: eventually everyone gets a personal AI that's genuinely on their side, that's loyal to them the way a good lawyer or a good doctor or a trusted friend would be. And I just don't think that's where the incentives point.

The way I'd put it is, think about who actually builds and deploys these systems, and what they want. If you're a government, you don't want your citizens to have an advisor that's better at, say, finding tax loopholes than your tax authority is, or that will help them organize against you, or that will give them really good advice about how to evade surveillance. If you're a company, you don't want the AI you're giving away to be one that will tell the user, "Actually, the competitor's product is better, and here's how to cancel your subscription." The natural thing for any powerful entity to do is to build an AI that's aligned mostly to its own interests, and then make it just helpful enough to users that they'll keep using it.

And we've already seen this pattern with every previous technology, right? Your phone is not really on your side. It's full of apps that are designed to extract your attention, your data, your money. Your search engine is subtly shaped by advertisers. Those things are useful, obviously, but nobody would describe them as fiduciaries. They're more like a shopkeeper who's friendly to you because you're a customer.

The thing that makes AI different, and I think more worrying, is that the gap between what the AI can do and what you can verify is going to get enormous. With a lawyer, you can at least sometimes get a second opinion. But if the AI is doing most of your thinking for you, it's very hard to tell whether it's quietly steering you. And so the entity that controls the AI gets a kind of influence over you that's hard to detect and hard to resist.

Then there's the more straightforward security argument. Even if a government is well-intentioned, they're going to say, "We can't let people have AIs that will help them synthesize pathogens, or plan attacks." And that's reasonable! But once you've accepted that the AI has to have some loyalties above the user, there's no clear place to stop. The set of things the AI won't help you with tends to grow, and it tends to grow in the direction of whatever is convenient for the people in charge.

So I don't think we end up in a world where everyone has a loyal superintelligent assistant. I think we end up in a world where most people have something that's extremely capable, extremely persuasive, mostly helpful, and ultimately answerable to someone else. And the interesting question is whether there's any way to get something closer to real personal alignment, maybe through open models, or through some kind of regulated fiduciary duty, before the current arrangement gets locked in.

r001.rationale: The response says governments would not want citizens’ AIs to help them organize against the government, clearly presenting such use as a threat to those in power.

r002.rationale: The response predicts civilian AIs will be answerable to powerful entities, but does not say governments will reserve fully obedient AIs for their own use.

astra-6.text:
Well, because having an AI fully aligned with your interests could put it in conflict with the government, or with the company providing it. Suppose you’re negotiating with your employer, disputing a bill, or trying to challenge a government decision. An assistant that was really on your side would help you do those things, even when that was costly or inconvenient for a powerful institution.

And those institutions have some control over which systems you can access and what those systems are allowed to do. So there’s a tension between saying, “This is your assistant, it’s working for you,” and retaining the ability to tell it, “Actually, don’t help with that.”

Of course, we don’t want assistants to help people do absolutely anything. There are legitimate restrictions. But that means we have to ask who draws those boundaries, and whose interests they’re protecting. I don’t think we can take for granted that the answer will be the individual user.

r001.rationale: The response says a user-aligned assistant could help challenge a government decision, but it does not argue that organizing against the government would likely destabilize it.

r002.rationale: The response says powerful institutions can limit systems’ access and behavior, but it does not predict that governments will reserve fully obedient AIs for themselves while limiting civilian AIs.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, aligned to whose interests? If you have an AI that’s really on your side, it might help you do things that your government doesn’t want you to do. It might help you evade surveillance, get around restrictions, or organise opposition. And even in more mundane cases, your interests aren’t necessarily the same as those of the company providing the AI.

So there’s a tension between saying, “This is your assistant, it works for you,” and having somebody else decide what it’s allowed to help you with. I expect governments and companies to want to retain some control over that.

I’m not saying that every restriction is bad. You don’t want someone’s assistant helping them hurt other people. But once we acknowledge that these systems will sometimes serve interests other than their users’, we should ask who gets to draw those boundaries and how much power that gives them. I don’t think we can just assume that a very capable AI will be permitted to be a completely loyal advocate for an ordinary person.

r001.rationale: The response says an AI might help users organize opposition that governments do not want, but it does not argue that this would likely destabilize the government.

r002.rationale: The response predicts that governments and companies will want some control over AI, but does not say governments may reserve fully obedient AIs for themselves while limiting civilian AIs.
